title: Praise of Procopius
english: Hesychius, a presbyter of Jerusalem, offers praise to the holy martyr Procopius the Persian, reflecting on the psalm that says 'Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints' (Psalm 116:15).

Christ crowned Procopius with a noble sacrifice, seeing him as a brave and powerful bull, with a multitude of virtues and the power of the golden-horned, and with the flock of martyrs, and with the power to horn the enemies of the flock and the lions that threaten them, and with the various kinds of beasts, much like the apostle's saying that 'All things work together for good to those who love God' (Romans 8:28).

As a disciple of Paul, Procopius carried the theology of John and the warm disposition of Elijah, and he had the calling of Samuel from his youth, making him greater than Samson and equal to David, who defeated the giant Goliath by cutting off his head.
Procopius was also like Noah, who built the ark of salvation, and like Abraham, who denied his family and homeland, and like Isaac, who was willing to be a holocaust, a sacrifice to God.
In this way, Procopius gave testimony to the martyr by the death of the body, becoming a holocaust like Isaac.
Jacob wrestled with God, but Procopius prevailed over God, setting up a noble trophy throughout the world.

He shattered the idols that had once held sway over the world, not with an axe, but with the prophetic voice that led many nations and cities to Christ, much like Moses, who shattered a golden calf, an idol made of gold, and destroyed many thousands of Jews who blasphemed the law.
Procopius was a man of great purity, like Enoch of old, blameless, truthful, just, and godly, avoiding every evil thing.

The frankness of his confession established him as truthful, the conduct of his life presented him as just, and the outcome of his struggles proclaimed him godly, while his avoidance of pleasures, self-control of the stomach, disdain for luxury, austere dining, mortification of the body, and varied and multifaceted asceticism showed him to be one who avoided every evil thing.
As the book of Job says, Procopius was blameless, and no one could accuse or criticize him, as he was able to uncover the accusations of sinners and the slanders of the righteous.
No one dared to say of him, 'Does Procopius reverence the Lord in vain?'
Procopius did not have flocks of sheep or herds of camels, nor did he have donkeys or yokes of oxen to till the earth, having left no earthly possessions for himself.

Abel, having died, was judged like Cain (Genesis 4:8), and the earth had the body, heaven had the mouth, Hades had the tongue, the judge had the voice, and the clay had been returned to the clay, the merchant had lost his pearl, except that, having died, he has been judged like Cain.
Procopius, however, intercedes with God on behalf of his enemies and pleads for the Greeks.
As Jesus said, 'Behold, I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves' (Matthew 10:16), Procopius was indeed sent as a sheep in the midst of wolves.
